documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) workloads are rapidly changing the energy landscape of today's data centers, both in terms of total electricity usage and power density at the facility level. The ongoing deployment of large-scale AI training and inference infrastructure is further driving and increasing the demand for electrical reliability, cooling capacity, power quality, grid interconnection, and low-carbon electricity supply. These interdependent issues require coordinated consideration of energy-infrastructure planning that takes into consideration renewable energy generation and storage, electrical architecture, operational flexibility, economic performance, and system resilience. The critical review combines 155 sources, mostly published between 2015 and 2026, identified and screened following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, which includes peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, technical standards, agency and institutional reports, market analyses, and corporate disclosure. The resulting evidence is presented in a seven-component decision framework that includes site and resource assessment, technology selection, electrical architecture, control and dispatch, workload flexibility, economic evaluation, and resilience and sustainability. The reviewed evidence indicates that renewable generation, energy storage, grid-support technologies, and workload flexibility can support lower-carbon AI data-center operations; however, the technical and economic performance of these approaches remains highly dependent on project-specific resource conditions, market structures, reliability requirements, and system boundaries. Reliability assessment requires a chronological, site-specific evaluation of load, resource, and infrastructure conditions. Wind–solar complementarity and workload flexibility may improve renewable-energy utilization; however, their benefits remain strongly dependent on operational and geographic constraints. The proposed framework is intended as a screening and decision-support tool rather than a prescriptive design methodology or site-specific optimization model. Important research needs include reproducible techno-economic assessment methods, independently verifiable corporate metrics, improved workload-flexibility characterization, and integrated evaluation of energy, water, reliability, and sustainability impacts. The resulting framework provides a structured basis for evaluating renewable-powered AI data center infrastructure across technical, economic, operational, and sustainability dimensions.

ABSTRACT This study investigates the efficacy of graphic recording, a real‐time visual facilitation technique, in mitigating information overload and enhancing training effectiveness within human resource development (HRD) and vocational education and training (VET) contexts. A quasi‐experimental design was implemented with 100 managers from a Taiwanese jewellery company operating in Thailand, randomly assigned to an experimental group ( n = 50) that received training accompanied by graphic recording and a control group ( n = 50) that did not. Post‐training surveys assessed trainee reactions (Kirkpatrick's Level 1), and a 10‐item multiple‐choice examination assessed learning acquisition (Kirkpatrick's Level 2). Hierarchical regression tested the moderating role of graphic recording on the relationship between information overload and training outcomes. Information overload was significantly and negatively associated with trainee reactions ( β = −0.352, p < 0.001) and with learning ( β = −0.550, p < 0.001). Graphic recording significantly moderated both relationships (ΔR² = 0.069 for reactions; ΔR² = 0.106 for learning; p < 0.05), with interaction plots showing flatter slopes for the experimental group, indicating that engagement and comprehension were sustained under high cognitive load. Grounded in cognitive load theory, dual‐coding theory, and visualisation theory, this study empirically validates graphic recording as a low‐cost, scalable alternative to virtual, augmented, or artificial‐intelligence‐based training technologies, and offers HRD and VET practitioners an evidence‐based, culturally inclusive tool for optimising training design in resource‐limited, cross‐national settings.

documents.abstract: This paper examines why historical and current protections have not consistently provided early recognition, diagnosis, treatment, return to service, or whole-of-life care for military and emergency services personnel affected by service-related psychological and physical harm. It applies Dmitry Nikolaenko’s three regimes of scientific recognition—Accompanying Science, Warning Science, and Critical Reconstruction—to New Zealand Defence Force and emergency services contexts. The analysis considers psychological trauma, moral injury, cumulative occupational stress, cancers, and other chronic conditions associated with repeated exposure to toxins, toxic environments, and temperature-related stressors. Evidence is drawn from New Zealand legislation, operational arrangements, official reports, published research, compensation processes, and existing health data systems. The paper argues that Nikolaenko’s model remains applicable when attention shifts from environmental contamination to human health, but that Critical Reconstruction does not by itself specify what must happen after institutional non-recognition has been identified. Two further regimes are therefore proposed. Critical Practice addresses immediate protection, monitoring, data preservation, redress, and operational change. Critical Regeneration redesigns the relationship between scientific inquiry, governance responsibility, law, occupational health, and operational practice so that future harm is recognized and acted on earlier. Together, the five regimes form the Nikolaenko-Alexander Model. Applied to New Zealand law and practice, the model identifies fragmented records, inconsistent legal coverage, high burdens of proof, and the absence of integrated long-term monitoring. It provides a framework for more equitable recognition, support, and precautionary governance.

documents.abstract: Reducing unsafe behavior among construction workers remains a central concern in construction management. While artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are increasingly adopted to replace or monitor workers, the negative perceptions workers hold toward the promotion of such technologies have largely been overlooked. This study introduces the concept of perceived risk with AI, defined as workers’ subjective perception of the potential negative consequences associated with AI adoption. Drawing on self-determination theory, which emphasizes individuals’ core psychological needs, we propose an inside-out theoretical model. This model explains how construction workers’ perceived risk with AI triggers unsafe behavior through two internal psychological pathways: emotional exhaustion and organizational identification. We further identify AI failure as a critical boundary condition that amplifies these effects. Data were collected from 343 frontline workers at 3 smart construction sites where AI actively interacts with human labor. Results indicate that perceived risk with AI increases unsafe behavior, and this relationship is mediated by both heightened emotional exhaustion and weakened organizational identification. Notably, these effects are significantly amplified when AI malfunctions occur. Our findings not only extend the application scope of self-determination theory but also contribute to the knowledge base on workers’ unsafe behavior in the context of human-AI coexistence. Practically, the study offers actionable insights for managers to mitigate the unintended side effects of AI implementation on worker safety.

documents.abstract: With its swift evolution, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has revolutionized the field of education, offering possibilities for personalized learning, automated grading, content generation, and administrative assistance. Large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT and Gemini, have revolutionized the way teachers and students engage in learning.Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and Gemini have transformed how teachers and students approach teaching and learning in schools and higher education institutions. Their pervasive use, however, brings many ethical questions about academic integrity, privacy, transparency, fairness, accountability, and human autonomy. This study investigates the ethical implications of the use of generative AI in education using a doctrinal and interdisciplinary method. It scans upto-date literature, international policy documents, and ethical guidelines that have been released from 2020 to 2026. Special focus is placed on algorithmic bias, data protection, intellectual property, digital inequality, misinformation, and learner reliance on AI systems. The results indicate that key elements of responsible AI governance need to be human-centred educational values, institutional accountability, AI literacy, and inclusive policy-making. The research suggests an ethical framework focusing on transparency, fairness, privacy protection, critical thinking, and collaborative governance to support the sustainable and responsible use of generative AI in education.

documents.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has raised important questions about how students evaluate the ethical implications of AI-assisted academic practices and whether those evaluations are linked to intentions to use these tools responsibly. While previous research has largely focused on technology adoption and acceptance, it has paid less attention to the relationship between ethical reasoning and intentions to use these tools responsibly. This study develops and tests an integrated framework that combines the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and moral cognition theory to examine how technology perceptions and academic and cognitive factors relate to students’ ethical reasoning and intentions to use ChatGPT responsibly. The study used a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design among business and management students in Oman and analysed the data using structural equation modelling. The findings indicate that perceived ease of use, academic pressure, and moral disengagement are positively associated with ethical reasoning, whereas perceived usefulness is not significantly associated with ethical reasoning. Ethical reasoning is positively associated with behavioural intention to use ChatGPT responsibly. In contrast, ChatGPT usage does not significantly moderate the relationship between academic pressure and ethical reasoning. These findings suggest that students’ responsible-use intentions are associated with their ethical evaluations of ChatGPT-assisted academic practices, while conventional technology acceptance perceptions and usage frequency alone offer a more limited explanation of ethical reasoning. The study contributes to emerging research on responsible generative AI use by extending TAM beyond conventional adoption outcomes and integrating it with a moral cognition perspective. It highlights the relationship between ethical reasoning and responsible-use intentions while distinguishing ethical evaluation from technology acceptance and usage frequency. The findings also provide context-specific evidence from Omani higher education, while recognising the limitations of the cross-sectional design, self-reported measures, and a context-specific sample.

documents.abstract: Burn injury is one of the leading causes of mortality worldwide, and dynamic prediction of in-hospital mortality during the patient’s hospital course can help identify patients at risk and support improved clinical management. While variables such as ICU length of stay and overall hospital length of stay are not known at admission, our models are intended to provide risk estimates that can be updated as these data become available, rather than serving as a static admission-time score. In this study, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models were implemented to predict mortality using a burn dataset comprising six key variables, including age, burn percentage, number of hospitalization days, number of ICU stay days, infection status, and gender. Multiple supervised learning algorithms, including ensemble tree-based methods and fully connected neural networks, were trained and evaluated using standard classification and discrimination metrics. In addition, to enhance model transparency, several explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including Shapley Additive explanations (SHAP), permutation importance, and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME), were applied. These analyses enabled the assessment of the importance, nonlinear risk patterns, and patient-level predictive behavior. Among all evaluated models, XGBoost achieved the highest discriminative performance, with a receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC) of 0.9896 and a precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC) of 0.9502, and was selected as the reference model for interpretability analyses. Several other ensemble tree-based methods, including Gradient Boosting Machine, Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), and Random Forest, also performed strongly, with ROC-AUC values exceeding 0.98. However, these results are based on internal validation from a single center; external validation is essential before clinical application.

This study investigates EFL learners’ attitudes toward using ChatGPT for English writing and examines the extent to which institutional and teacher-related factors predict these attitudes. In this quantitative study, a survey questionnaire was administered to 136 preparatory-year EFL students in a Saudi higher-education context. Descriptive analysis indicated that learners held generally positive attitudes toward ChatGPT for English writing. Participants also reported moderately positive perceptions of institutional support and teachers’ attitudes, although limited training and classroom integration were noted. Multiple regression analysis revealed that institution-related factors significantly predicted learners’ attitudes toward ChatGPT use, whereas teacher-related factors did not demonstrate a unique predictive contribution when both variables were considered simultaneously. The study contributes empirical evidence from the Saudi EFL context and extends prior descriptive research by identifying contextual predictors of attitudes toward AI-assisted writing. Implications emphasize the importance of clear institutional policies, AI literacy initiatives, and targeted teacher training to support responsible integration of ChatGPT in language learning.

Abstract Background The rapid emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping medical education worldwide. However, existing studies are predominantly quantitative and Western-centric providing limited empirical evidence regarding how medical sciences faculty members and students experience and interpret the use of AI within constrained educational and socio-cultural contexts. This study aimed to explore the experiences of medical sciences faculty and students regarding AI use at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences, Iran. Methods A qualitative descriptive study was conducted from November 2024 to April 2025. A total of 16 participants (eight faculty members and eight students) from diverse medical disciplines with prior AI experience recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Data were collected through semi‑structured, in‑depth interviews (50–60 min) supported by field notes and continued until data saturation was achieved. Interviews were transcribed verbatim and analyzed using Graneheim and Lundman’s qualitative content analysis with MAXQDA 24. Trustworthiness was ensured through qualitative rigor criteria, following COREQ guidelines. Results Five overarching themes with 16 subthemes emerged from the study: 1) functional and practical value of AI; 2) human oversight, ethics and authenticity; 3) perceived capacity building and institutional readiness; 4) cognitive, emotional, and behavioral influence; and 5) socio-cultural dynamics and future transformation. However, participants’ experiences varied based on their roles: faculty members used AI strategically for routine tasks preserving cognitive effort for more complex ones, whereas students exhibited a more relational reliance on AI, which appeared to increase their vulnerability to automation bias. Both groups expressed concerns about potential "intellectual deskilling" and infrastructure barriers, conceptualized as a geopolitical algorithmic divide that limits equitable access. Conclusions The experiences of AI use among medical sciences faculty and students are context-dependent and conditional rather than uniformly positive or negative. Its sustainable integration into medical education involves a complex negotiation between efficiency and significant ethical, cognitive and institutional challenges. these findings highlight the potential need for a pedagogical shift toward evaluative judgment and institutional support to bridge the geopolitical digital divide, alongside human-in-the-loop supervision to help mitigate the risk of educational deskilling. Future longitudinal research is recommended to explore how perceptions, ethical concerns, and usage patterns evolve as AI becomes more embedded in medical education.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial Intelligence (AI), with its range of applications and ease of use, is transforming medicine. AI usage is increasing exponentially in a resource-limited country like Pakistan; however, application in medical education is evolving and needs to be understood. Little work has been done on perceptions among faculty and students to understand their understanding and readiness to use AI, while keeping in mind the ethical issues it may raise. Objective: To explore perceptions of faculty and students regarding integration of AI into undergraduate medical education, potential challenges and ethical considerations in adoption of AI, at a public sector university in Pakistan. Methods: Exploratory descriptive qualitative study at Dow University of Health Sciences, Karachi, from October 2025 to March 2026, including faculty in-depth interviews (IDI) and focus group discussions (FGD) with MBBS students till data saturation was achieved. Audio recording and transcription were done using an artificial intelligence tool. Data were thematically analyzed using the Braun and Clarke framework. Results: A total of 10 IDIs and 5 FGDs were conducted. IDIs included 10 faculty members: 6 (60%) females and 4 (40%) males, aged 38-55 years. FGDs included 40 students (males: 15, females: 25), with 7-8 participants per FGD, aged 20-25 years. Six key themes were derived: Modernization in Education, Curriculum Integration, Clinical Research and Practice, Ethics and Professional Responsibility, Readiness of the Institute, Strategic Integration, and Governance Issues. Conclusion: Faculty and students see AI as a supportive tool that increases access to healthcare and information and reduces errors. Important concerns raised included confidentiality, privacy, and fear of AI replacing humans in the medical sector.

documents.abstract: This work introduces Field-Wave Algebra (FWA), a mathematical framework that models reality as a system of dynamic field states, error-driven evolution, and recursive return processes. Instead of treating numbers, matter, consciousness, and information as isolated static entities, FWA describes them as manifestations of continuous field dynamics. The framework is built around the relationship between structural deviation, error magnitude, and return operators, expressed through a fundamental consciousness equation and a hierarchy of evolving system states. The model spans inert matter, biological organisms, artificial intelligence, and large-scale cosmic structures within a unified formalism. A central concept of FWA is the loop structure 0 → S → 0, where systems evolve away from equilibrium and attempt to restore balance through recursive feedback mechanisms. Error is interpreted not as a defect but as a generative force driving adaptation, complexity, and emergent organization. The paper presents mathematical foundations for dynamic state evolution, field correction processes, self-organization, and number resonance. Artificial intelligence is analyzed as an open-loop architecture capable of state generation but lacking autonomous loop closure. Numbers are interpreted as active wave resonances rather than static symbols, leading to a process-oriented view of mathematics. FWA proposes a unified perspective linking consciousness, dynamic systems, information processing, error propagation, and mathematical structure within a single field-based framework.

Higher art education is undergoing a significant transformation as traditional models of disciplinary and technical formation increasingly intersect with artistic autonomy, research-oriented practice, interdisciplinary learning, and artificial intelligence (AI). The article examines how educational structures and institutional cultures shape the formation of artists and designers, focusing comparatively on France and Armenia. The relevance of the topic is determined by the need to understand how contemporary institutions organise the transition from disciplinary knowledge toward independent creative agency at a moment when AI is reshaping established understandings of technical skill, authorship, and artistic decision-making. The aim of the study is to determine how different educational cultures shape the development of artistic autonomy, artistic identity, and research capacity in higher art education, and how these relationships might be transformed by artificial intelligence. The research methods are based on a comparative socio-pedagogical approach combining documentary analysis, institutional observation, curriculum analysis, and qualitative interpretation. The empirical component draws primarily on field study conducted in Saint-Étienne, France, during 2024–2025, with particular attention to the École Supérieure d'Art et Design de Saint-Étienne (ESADSE) and Université Jean Monnet, while Armenian higher art education is examined as a comparative context. The analysis is informed by Pierre Bourdieu's concept of cultural production, Michel Foucault's understanding of disciplinary formation, and the concept of artistic research. The scientific novelty of the study lies in the comparative socio-pedagogical analysis of French and Armenian higher art education as distinct educational cultures, in interpreting artistic formation as a movement from disciplinary learning toward increasing autonomy and research capacity, and in extending this framework to the relationship between artistic autonomy and artificial intelligence. The results indicate that both French and Armenian systems recognise the importance of technical and professional competence but organise the transition toward artistic autonomy differently. The French programmes examined show a more explicit progression from foundational education toward specialisation, individual projects, experimentation, professional engagement, and research-oriented practice. Armenian higher art education retains a stronger continuity with systematic technical and disciplinary formation, while incorporating comparable Bachelor–Master–Doctoral structures. Conclusions. Technical competence and artistic autonomy should not be treated as opposing educational objectives; contemporary art education requires a productive transition between disciplinary knowledge and independent creative agency. The emergence of AI further complicates this relationship by shifting attention from technical execution toward conceptual thinking, critical judgement, authorship, research capacity, and ethical responsibility. For Armenian higher art education, the findings suggest an approach based on adaptation rather than imitation, combining established traditions of technical formation with greater opportunities for specialisation, artistic research, professional practice, digital literacy, and responsible human–AI creative engagement.

This review examines the conceptual architecture and methodological implications of the dialogic reading framework as proposed in "From Distant to Dialogic Reading: Large Language Models and the Methodological Reconfiguration of Literary Criticism." The framework advances a timely intervention in digital literary studies by proposing a shift from the extractive logic of distant reading to a dialogic mode in which large language models function not as instruments of pattern detection but as interlocutors in a recursive hermeneutic process. Situating the framework within the broader scholarly conversation surrounding AI and literary interpretation, this review evaluates its theoretical foundations, methodological rigor, and empirical grounding. The framework draws on Bakhtinian dialogism, Eco's theory of the open work, and the functionalist stance in AI criticism to provide a vocabulary for treating machine-generated interpretations as provocations rather than pronouncements. However, the review argues that while the framework's central thesis offers a productive reconceptualization of computational criticism's aims, its contribution remains primarily programmatic. The absence of controlled comparison, the underspecification of criteria for interpretive value, and the insufficient engagement with critical AI scholarship collectively limit its immediate applicability. The Barthes–Eco Simulation, while pedagogically suggestive, does not demonstrate that dialogic reading produces insights unavailable through conventional methods. The review identifies three requirements for operationalizing dialogic reading as a testable methodology: specifying the conditions under which LLM outputs contribute interpretive surplus rather than algorithmic positivity; developing criteria for evaluating human-machine interpretive collaboration; and conducting controlled comparisons against established methods on common corpora. The hermeneutic hypercycle model offers one promising template for such empirical work. The framework provides the conceptual scaffolding; the harder work of building and testing the structure remains.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly evolving and creating new possibilities for supporting students' entrepreneurial development. However, limited research has examined how GAI usage is associated with entrepreneurial intention (EI) through specific psychological pathways. Drawing on self-efficacy theory, this study examines the relationship between GAI usage and EI, focusing on the mediating roles of task and social self-efficacy. Using survey data from 521 Chinese university students, this study empirically tests the proposed model. The results show that GAI usage is positively associated with students' task and social self-efficacy. However, task self-efficacy (TSE) is not directly associated with EI. In contrast, social self-efficacy (SSE) accounts for a significant indirect association between GAI usage and EI. Moreover, a significant sequential indirect association is observed, linking GAI usage with EI through TSE and SSE. By disentangling the distinct roles of TSE and SSE, this study shows that the association between GAI usage and EI is consistent with pathways that differ in their functions and proximity to entrepreneurial action. The findings also provide practical insights for entrepreneurship education and AI-supported learning environments.

Generative artificial intelligence is reaching small firms in emerging economies with unusual speed, because it is rented, not built, and is operated through ordinary language instead of code. This paper develops a conceptual framework that explains when and how generative AI use improves innovation performance in emerging-economy small and medium-sized enterprises. Drawing on absorptive capacity, dynamic capabilities and the institution-based view, and on the resource-based view for the diffusion argument, the framework treats generative AI as a low-cost conduit to codified external knowledge whose innovation value depends on the firm's capacity to verify, transform and exploit what the technology produces. Eight propositions, two of them stated as pairs and so ten statements in all, specify the mechanisms and boundary conditions. Generative AI is expected to widen knowledge access most where external knowledge networks are weakest, to strengthen sensing and the design elements of seizing more than transforming, and to favour incremental product and service innovation, process innovation within existing operations, business model innovation and innovation speed over novel product innovation. Its effect is moderated at the firm level by the evaluative expertise of the owner-manager and core staff, and bounded by the type of institutional void the firm faces, by an infrastructure and affordability threshold, by the fit between the model's training data and the firm's language and market context, and by the stage of diffusion among competing firms. As use diffuses, advantage shifts from access to the combination of generative AI with idiosyncratic local knowledge. The paper treats generative AI as a substitute for the channels through which these firms have obtained external knowledge and a complement to the firm's own evaluative expertise, and sets out a research agenda for testing the framework.

Academics need both an overarching policy on Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) use in teaching and learning, yet agency in its application across various disciplines. Clarity on the use of the technology for both students and staff is therefore a challenge and characterised by uncertainty given how its application is still unfamiliar. This research examines the organisational context in which Gen AI is being embraced and was conducted by the digital teaching support functions within an Irish university. Students and staff were surveyed (n=1,746) on various aspects of digital use within their education and workplace, including Gen AI. This data explored to what extent staff and students are adopting the technology in their work and study, which tools they use and importantly what guidance they received. The university statement of intent identifies that it acknowledges that students and staff are already using AI tools and that it is supportive of the legitimate and appropriate application of such tools once university policies are adhered to. This research probes into the extent that this ambition is achieved on the ground and how guidance is being interpreted while maintaining the integrity of academic work.

documents.abstract: Misinformation refers to false, inaccurate, or misleading information that can significantly influence public opinion, decision-making, and societal behaviour. With the rapid growth of social media and online communication platforms, the large-scale dissemination of misinformation has become a critical challenge, highlighting the need for effective automated detection techniques. This survey presents a comprehensive review of recent advances in misinformation detection by examining the complete detection pipeline, including information representation, event detection, semantic similarity analysis, information verification, and classification methods. It reviews conventional machine learning, deep learning, graph-based, and transformer-based approaches that have been proposed for identifying misinformation across diverse application domains. Furthermore, widely used benchmark datasets are analysed, and the performance characteristics of representative detection models are compared to highlight their strengths and limitations. The survey also identifies current research challenges, including data quality, explainability, domain adaptation, multimodal misinformation, and model generalisation, and discusses promising future research directions. By providing a structured overview of existing methodologies, datasets, and emerging trends, this survey serves as a comprehensive reference for researchers and practitioners working in misinformation detection and trustworthy artificial intelligence.

Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a crucial task to estimate the probability that users will click on items in online platforms. Recently, researchers have incorporated semantics derived from large language models (LLMs) into representations of users and items in graph neural networks (GNNs) framework to facilitate CTR prediction. However, existing hybrid GNNs-LLMs models predominantly treat GNNs and LLMs as two independent components, and suffer from the ineffective modality alignment between graph and textual representations. To address these issues, we propose LLMs-enhanced GNNs for CTR prediction (GraphLLM4CTR), where LLMs coordinate message passing in GNNs by infusing layer-wise semantics into message updates and graph representation learning. Specifically, we design a multi-view contrastive alignment (MVCA) method to transform graph and prompt-based embeddings into modality-aware representations and achieve modality alignment through intra-view and inter-view contrastive learning. Moreover, we propose a LLMs-based message coordinator (LBMC) that projects graph representations into an aligned latent space and incorporates LLMs with learnable adapters to regulate semantic-injected graph representation learning. Subsequently, we present a hybrid-expert mechanism with gating networks to adaptively aggregate representations for CTR prediction. Experiments conducted on three public datasets (i.e., MovieLens-1M, BookCrossing, and Amazon-Sports) demonstrate the superiority of GraphLLM4CTR over state-of-the-art baselines in terms of AUC and Logloss, and validate the adaptability of MVCA to topological properties and of LBMC to text qualities, and the dynamic balance of the hybrid-expert mechanism. Finally, we conduct analysis of space and time complexity, and computational efficiency of GraphLLM4CTR during training and inference stages, which indicates that GraphLLM4CTR can achieve the optimal AUC-latency trade-off and a linear scalability with the number of nodes and of edges in constructed graphs.

This study examines strategic retrofitting in high-end artistic ceramics manufacturing under stringent “Dual Carbon” regulations. Balancing regulatory compliance with artisanal integrity represents a significant industrial challenge. To address this multidimensional problem, this research develops an integrated hybrid multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) framework combining the Full Consistency Method (FUCOM) and the Measurement of Alternatives and Ranking according to Compromise Solution (MARCOS). Gemini 1.5 Pro was employed exclusively as a “Synthetic Knowledge Engineer” to extract and organise candidate criteria from five authoritative regulatory and technical documents, which were subsequently validated and refined by a multidisciplinary human expert panel to construct the Evaluation Index System (EIS). FUCOM results indicate that “Environmental Compliance and Process Monitoring” is the most influential main criterion, while “Specific Energy Intensity”, “Weighted Flue Gas Emissions” and “Payback Period and ROI” emerge as the most important sub-criteria. The MARCOS evaluation identifies the “Hybrid Evolutionary Path” as the highest-ranked compromise pathway, reflecting a phased investment strategy that balances emission reduction objectives with capital constraints. Sensitivity analyses and comparative assessments using established MCDM methods, including TOPSIS, COPRAS, WASPAS and VIKOR, demonstrate a high degree of ranking stability under the tested analytical conditions. The proposed framework provides a transparent and potentially transferable decision-support approach to facilitate low-carbon transitions in traditional craft-based manufacturing industries.

documents.abstract: Background: Occupational hazards remain an important concern among healthcare workers, particularly in resource-limited primary healthcare settings where inadequate protective equipment, heavy workloads and limited occupational health support may increase exposure risks. Although healthcare workers may have good knowledge of occupational hazards, this knowledge does not always translate into consistent safety practices. Evidence on this knowledge–practice gap among primary healthcare workers in Nigeria remains limited. Aims: To assess occupational hazard exposure, knowledge of occupational hazards and safety practices among healthcare workers in primary healthcare centres, and to examine whether the level of hazard exposure was associated with the level of safety practice. Study Design: Descriptive cross-sectional study. Place and Duration of Study: Two government-owned primary healthcare centres in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, Nigeria, between April 2026 and June 2026. Methodology: A structured self-administered questionnaire was completed by 124 clinical and non-clinical healthcare workers selected by proportionate allocation and simple random sampling. Hazard exposure, knowledge and safety practice were measured on five-point Likert scales and classified from composite scores. The association between exposure level and practice level was tested with Pearson’s chi-square and the Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact test. Results: Most respondents were female (64.5%) and aged 45 years or older (51.6%). Exposure was reported across all hazard categories; 71.0% agreed that they had experienced a needlestick or sharps injury, 64.5% reported exposure to blood or body fluids, and 61.3% reported work-related stress. Overall, 62.1% had high hazard exposure. Knowledge was good in 97.6% of respondents, yet only 16.1% agreed that they consistently used personal protective equipment and 18.5% that they regularly practised hand hygiene. Overall, 79.0% had fair and 15.3% good safety practice. Heavy workload was the most strongly endorsed barrier (58.1% agreement). Safety practice level was not associated with hazard exposure level (χ² = 2.383, df = 2, p = 0.304; exact p = 0.316). Conclusion: Healthcare workers in these centres knew the risks well but did not consistently apply basic protective measures, and workers with high exposure practised no more safely than those with moderate exposure. Improving safety in primary care is therefore likely to depend on equipment supply, staffing and supportive supervision more than on further awareness training.

documents.abstract: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the workplace underscores the urgent need to understand how employees collaborate effectively with AI systems. Grounded in social cognitive theory, this study investigates the impact of empowering leadership on employee–AI collaboration. Furthermore, we examine the mediating roles of psychological safety and AI trust. Design/methodology/approach To test the research model, we utilized a multilevel design data from 418 employees across 103 teams in AI-integrated organizations in Vietnam. Findings Our findings indicate that empowering leadership is positively related to employee–AI collaboration, with this relationship mediated by both psychological safety and AI trust. Originality/value This study contributes to the leadership and technology management literature by establishing a multilevel link between empowering leadership and employee–AI collaboration. It identifies key mediating mechanisms (AI trust and psychological safety), offering a more integrated understanding of leadership influence in AI-enabled settings. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for practitioners navigating the dynamics of employee–AI collaboration, highlighting the importance of empowering leadership in building AI-ready workforces.

documents.abstract: Purpose We investigate whether the adoption of conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) translates corporate complexity into clearer financial narratives. CAI, representing AI-driven innovation, can bolster operational efficiency and performance, thereby leading to better financial transparency and readability of financial statement information. Design/methodology/approach We construct a firm-level CAI measure from CAI-related disclosures in 10-K filings using Sent-latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA)-variational expectation maximization (VEM) topic modelling. Our measure captures CAI applications related to service and operations, and decision-making and governance. We also use patent-based measures based on natural language processing and speech-recognition technologies as alternative proxies in robustness tests. Findings We find that CAI adoption is associated with lower Bog Index scores, indicating more readable 10-K reports. Mediation tests show that financial performance and operational efficiency partially mediate this relationship. The results remain robust after addressing endogeneity concerns and using alternative specifications. Originality/value Using unsupervised machine learning topic modelling, we observe that CAI is predominantly employed in corporate operations, notably in service-related activities, decision-making processes and corporate governance.

Collaborative Problem Solving (CPS) constitutes an important competence for pre-service teachers. However, fostering their deep engagement in such tasks remains a persistent challenge. Drawing upon self-determination theory and flow theory, the present study introduced an innovative gamification mechanism into a university classroom and integrated it with the flipped classroom approach. A nine-week quasi-experiment was implemented with 40 pre-service teachers in China. Data were collected through pre- and post-intervention surveys on learning motivation and flow experience and video recordings of collaborative sessions. Quantitative data were analysed using paired-samples t-tests, while video data were examined using Lag Sequential Analysis (LSA) to identify significant behavioural transitions in the CPS process. Results showed that intrinsic motivation and flow significantly improved. LSA revealed that CPS patterns evolved positively under game elements, including more efficient knowledge construction, more critical solution testing and more effective social interactions. Limitations and future directions are discussed.

Artificial Intelligence is increasingly capable of performing cognitive work that was previously associated primarily with human intellectual ability. Generative AI can now assist with writing, analysis, reasoning, coding, interpretation, and decision support, allowing individuals to produce sophisticated intellectual outputs that may exceed their independently demonstrated understanding. As a result, the quality of human output may become an increasingly incomplete indicator of the cognitive capability genuinely possessed by the human producing it.This conceptual opinion paper proposes Human Genuine Intelligence (HGI) as a framework for examining this emerging distinction. HGI refers to the cognitive capacity that humans genuinely possess, understand, and exercise through question formation, independent reasoning, analytical thinking, evidence evaluation, causal understanding, judgment, and cognitive revision.The paper introduces Borrowed Intelligence (BI) and the Cognitive Dependency Gap (CDG) as conceptual lenses for examining potential mismatches between AI-augmented capability and independently accountable human cognitive capability. Rather than advocating reduced use of AI, it proposes Active Cognitive Augmentation (ACA) as a model for human–AI interaction: THINK → ASK → AUGMENT → CHALLENGE → VERIFY → REVISE → DECIDE WITH WISDOM.The paper further argues that cognitive capability alone is insufficient for navigating increasingly powerful AI systems. HGI therefore needs to be considered alongside Human Wisdom, which provides direction and responsibility, and Cognitive Sovereignty, which concerns the preservation of human agency and authority over consequential goals, values, delegation boundaries, and decisions.The central challenge of the AI age is therefore not to preserve human intelligence by limiting artificial intelligence, but to strengthen human cognition, wisdom, and agency while using increasingly capable machines.

documents.abstract: Expanded working paper proposing a six-dimension framework for evaluating control failures in advanced AI agents: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. Version 1.2 retains the pilot cases and severity framework and adds related work, evidence-discovery and provenance procedures, continuity-seeking analysis, consciousness and moral-status uncertainty, Apple Full Disk Access permission analysis, and a prepared independent coding and remediation protocol. The Apple announcement is not treated as proof of a Muse permission bypass. This is a conceptual, unreviewed working paper; no independent coding results or completed validation are claimed. It is a substantive expansion of the available manuscript, not a recovered copy of the inaccessible earlier longer draft. See the accompanying revision notes.

AI incident databases and risk taxonomies are increasingly valuable, but they often answer broad questions about harm, misuse, or system failure rather than the narrower operational question of whether humans remain meaningfully in control of increasingly agentic systems. This paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for analyzing agent-control failures: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. The framework separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. This v1.1 revision updates the paper title to better distinguish the work while preserving the Human in Control project name, the existing Human Control Model, the six-dimension framework, the original version lineage, and the publication record family. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. The prepared local export updates the recoverable v1.0.1 manuscript title and metadata; the prior longer sandbox-only v1.1 manuscript was unavailable. Creator: Human in Control Project. documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to deliver financial information, investment recommendations and portfolio decision support. This study examines the proposed impact of AI-based financial advice on investment preferences and risk perception among salaried investors. The framework treats perceived usefulness, perceived accuracy, trust, personalisation and transparency as dimensions of AI-based financial advice and tests their proposed relationships with investment preference and risk perception. A quantitative cross-sectional design using a structured five-point Likert questionnaire is proposed. For demonstration of the intended empirical reporting format, a synthetic dataset of 450 hypothetical salaried investors was generated and analysed using internal-consistency assessment and regression-style structural estimates. The simulated results indicate positive associations between the five AI-advice attributes and investment preference and negative associations with risk perception. These numerical findings are illustrative only and must not be represented as observations from real respondents. The study contributes a focused framework for future primary research on AI-assisted investment decision-making among salaried investors.

Abstract It is evident that Artificial Intelligence (AI) now plays and important role in every students life. It is being adapted progressively becoming an inevitable part of almost every student’s academic performance. The use of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Canva, and many more AI-based learning platforms support student learning effectively. These tools aid as search engine machines used to extract information. Students often use AI learning based platforms for synthezising challenging concepts, seeking creative assignment ideas. They also use AI tools for taming writing skills and specifically during preparation of their exam preparation. Generation Z, is known to be digitally native so they have grown up in an environment which is highly digital in nature. So they are highly privileged to secure an environment that not only supports but also openly accepts wide usage of AI based technologies. This adoption of AI based technology learning not only designs their day to day living easy, but also supports them in their learning processes. AI tools facilitate learning quicker in less time and features personalised learning. AI based learning tools are easily accessible for students as they are either free of cost or offered to students at lower costs. Although excessive dependence on AI based tools for learning is not fit for students as, it restricts their independent critical thinking blocking their creativity minds and hinders problem-solving abilities. The main purpose of the research paper was to scrutinize the impact of AI tools on the learning behaviour of Gen Z students. The study is an attempt to focus on gauging the frequency with which the Gen Z students use AI learning tools, understanding the purpose of AI usage. An analysis is done through to pivot lenses on the influence of AI based learning on various parameters like learning efficiency, change academic engagement, and the perception of students. It will give a clear picture whether students hold AI based learning as an advantage or a possible limitation when adopted for educational purposes.
